description: We are high-school students joining in for the fun of it!!
summary: Mars hardware is tested on Earth first, but analog sites are usually chosen by how they look. We measured them instead. Using ten years of NASA POWER climate data for 14 sites and 4,717 sols of Curiosity rover weather from Gale Crater, we score how closely each site, in each month, matches Mars, and which equipment failure it can test: cold soak, freeze-thaw, thermal cycling, winter power or panel dust. The result is an interactive 3D globe and animation. We found that Mongolia in January closes 66 to 70% of the climate gap to Mars, ahead of the Mars Society station in Utah (54%) and the Atacama (33%). It is the winter cold, not the Gobi desert, that does this, and by July the same sites fall to 1 to 19%. A test site is a place and a month.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

"How Martian is Mongolia?" is a web tool that shows where on Earth, and in which month, equipment would fail the way it would on Mars. The user picks a failure test and a month. A 3D globe raises a spike at each of 14 sites, and a panel shows that site's measurements beside Curiosity's measurements at Gale Crater. An animation then plays a full year of each failure: every dot is a night and every bar is a day, counted from the data.

HOW IT WORKS

We compared 14 sites: seven in Mongolia (Khorgo volcanic field, Ulaanbaatar, Uvs Nuur Basin, Tsagaan Suvarga, Khongoryn Els, Bayanzag, Khermen Tsav), six established analogs (McMurdo Dry Valleys, Haughton Crater, Qaidam Basin, the Mars Desert Research Station in Utah, the Atacama Desert, Mauna Loa) and Washington DC as an ordinary baseline.

Climate match uses five measurements: mean temperature, day-night swing, share of nights below freezing, air moisture and precipitation. Each is placed on a line from Washington DC's ten-year average (0%) to Gale Crater (100%), capped at both ends, and the five are averaged.

Each failure test reads one measured quantity:

- Cold soak: share of nights below -20 °C.

- Freeze-thaw: share of days whose air temperature crosses 0 °C.

- Thermal cycling: day-night swing as a share of Gale Crater's 62.3 K.

- Winter power: share of nights below -20 °C, counted only in months with a daily sunrise and sunlight no stronger than Mars receives.

- Panel dust: aerosol optical depth.

Rover traction is shown as "no data", because climate records cannot measure soil.

WHAT WE FOUND

- In January the seven Mongolian sites close 66 to 70% of the gap to Gale Crater. Only the polar deserts score higher (McMurdo Dry Valleys 76%, Haughton Crater 74%). The Utah station peaks at 54% and the Atacama at 33%.

- The four Gobi sites (66 to 68%) score no higher than Ulaanbaatar (69%) or Khorgo (70%). The local claim that the Gobi is Earth's most Mars-like desert is half right: the winter does the work, not the desert.

- By July the same sites close only 1 to 19%.

- Each failure has its own best site. Khorgo in January has 85% of nights below -20 °C and held that for 58 nights in a row; the Utah station never gets that cold. Tsagaan Suvarga is Mongolia's best site for freeze-thaw (October), thermal cycling (May) and dust (July).

WHERE THE ANALOGY BREAKS

We state the limits on the site. Earth's air is 89 to 124 times thicker than Gale Crater's. The widest day-night swing in our data is 16.5 K against 62 K on Mars. Only 3 of the 14 sites ever recorded a night below -40 °C, and every measured night at Gale was colder. Mars's 2018 dust storm was about 21 times dustier than our dustiest month. Gravity, carbon dioxide air and radiation are outside this data. The tool shows where to stress-test hardware, not whether it will survive.

BENEFITS

Engineers and analog-mission planners can choose a test site and month by the failure they need to provoke. For Mongolia, it gives a measured basis for winter analog testing.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python for the analysis; HTML, CSS and JavaScript with three.js for the site. The site is a single self-contained file, and every number on it is computed from the source files at build time.

Each of the five measurements is capped between 0% and 100% before averaging. Without the cap, a site that is wetter or milder than Washington DC scores below zero on that measurement (Mauna Loa's yearly score would be -28%), and one strongly negative measurement would hide how well the others match. The cap changes only the scoring, not the NASA data. Its effect is small where it matters: the seven Mongolian sites score 66 to 70% in January with or without it. It raises the best month of McMurdo Dry Valleys from 74% to 76%, Haughton Crater from 72% to 74% and the Atacama from 26% to 33%. All figures in this project use the capped score.
